query_text: How do judges generally decide if a lawsuit has gone on for too long, and what kinds of reasons do they consider when deciding whether to throw it out or remove any property holds connected to it?
answer:
Based on the provided evidence, when deciding whether to dismiss a lawsuit for having gone on for too long, courts in New Brunswick have consistently applied a three-part test. The party asking for the dismissal must establish that there has been an inordinate delay, that the delay is inexcusable, and that they are likely to be seriously prejudiced by the delay (Province of New Brunswick v Clayco Construction (2001) Ltd., et al; McNichol v. Co-operators General Insurance Co.).

Courts have found delays ranging from over seven to ten years to be inordinate (Province of New Brunswick v Clayco Construction (2001) Ltd., et al; McNichol v. Co-operators General Insurance Co.). Whether a delay is excusable depends on the specific reasons provided. For instance, in one case, a plaintiff’s deteriorating medical condition, cognitive issues, and family crises were accepted as a sufficient excuse for a ten-year delay (McNichol v. Co-operators General Insurance Co.). In another case, a government department's excuses that it was understaffed, dealing with other large files, and had changed solicitors were rejected as inexcusable, with the judge concluding the case was simply not a priority for them (Province of New Brunswick v Clayco Construction (2001) Ltd., et al).

Serious prejudice has been established where the delay impairs a party's ability to defend themselves. The clearest example of this was the death of a key witness who had personal, day-to-day knowledge of the project at the heart of the lawsuit (Province of New Brunswick v Clayco Construction (2001) Ltd., et al). The party claiming prejudice generally has the burden to prove it; a motion was denied where the defendant provided no evidence of any prejudice whatsoever (Levesque v Vitalité Health Network (Restigouche Health Authority-RSS5)). Some cases have stated that in instances of extreme or grossly inordinate delay, serious prejudice can be presumed, shifting the burden to the plaintiff to prove there is no prejudice (Province of New Brunswick v Clayco Construction (2001) Ltd., et al; McNichol v. Co-operators General Insurance Co.). However, at least one judge has expressed skepticism about this presumption, emphasizing that the party asking for dismissal must typically establish all three parts of the test, including prejudice (Levesque v Vitalité Health Network (Restigouche Health Authority-RSS5)). Overall, the courts view dismissing an action as a draconian remedy to be used with great caution and only in the clearest of cases (Régie régionale de la santé 6, Dr. Blanchard and Dr. Bélisle v. Robichaud).

When deciding whether to remove a property hold, referred to as a Certificate of Pending Litigation (CPL), the courts have applied a different and very stringent test. A CPL will only be removed if the property owner can prove that "under no possible circumstances" can the plaintiff's claim, if successful, give them an interest in that specific property (MacPhee v. Macphee Estate). This is a very high bar to meet. For example, a court refused to remove a CPL where the plaintiff's potential interest in the land was described as "remote" but still a "possibility" (MacPhee v. Macphee Estate). In another matter, a CPL was kept in place because the plaintiffs were asking the court to void the property sale and grant them the right to purchase it, a form of relief that would be lost if the CPL was removed and the property was sold to someone else (Michaud v. Saucier).

The provided evidence is insufficient to determine if delay is a significant factor when a judge decides whether to remove a CPL. In one case where a defendant argued the plaintiff had delayed for many years, the judge’s decision to keep the CPL did not mention the delay, focusing instead entirely on whether it was possible for the plaintiff to obtain an interest in the land (MacPhee v. Macphee Estate). The weight, if any, that a judge might give to a long delay in a CPL-removal application could be an important factor, but the provided evidence does not address it.

query_text: Given a pending motion to dismiss for lack of prosecution, citing a multi-year delay, what procedural steps should be taken to oppose it, particularly when the delay is attributable to factors such as multiple changes in counsel, pandemic-related court closures, and the death of a key witness? Furthermore, what are the available procedural mechanisms to challenge or vacate a lis pendens or similar encumbrance on real property that is currently tying up the client's land, especially when the underlying litigation is subject to a motion for dismissal?
answer:
Based on the provided evidence, when courts consider a motion to dismiss for delay, they consistently apply a three-part test. The party bringing the motion must establish that there has been (1) an inordinate delay, (2) the delay is inexcusable, and (3) the delay is likely to cause serious prejudice to the defendant (Province of New Brunswick v Clayco Construction, para 22; Francis v LeBlanc, para 20). The dismissal of an action for delay is considered a drastic remedy to be exercised with caution and only in the clearest of cases (Province of New Brunswick v Clayco Construction, para 24; Régie régionale de la santé 6 v. Robichaud, para 35).

Regarding the factors for delay mentioned in the query:

Courts have found multi-year delays to be inordinate. For example, a delay of nearly six years where the action had not moved past pleadings was found to be grossly inordinate (Francis v LeBlanc, para 21). Whether a delay is inordinate is specific to the circumstances of each case (Province of New Brunswick v Clayco Construction, para 25).

The pandemic has been recognized by courts as a potential excuse for delay. The chaos caused by the COVID-19 pandemic was considered an exigent circumstance that justified an extension of time, despite significant concerns about the delay (Bridgewater Bank v. Pietersma, para 22). In other contexts, delays due to COVID-19 have been treated as "discrete exceptional circumstances" that justify delay, taking into account court closures and case backlogs (S.J.L. v. R., para 40; His Majesty the King v. Darrin Albert Donovan, para 31). However, one court noted that a pandemic-based excuse would have been more persuasive if the party had acted more promptly after the courts became fully functional again (Bridgewater Bank v. Pietersma, para 21).

The evidence regarding changes in counsel suggests that while courts may be sympathetic, the ultimate responsibility to advance the litigation rests with the plaintiff. In Francis v LeBlanc, the court granted an adjournment to allow the plaintiff to find new counsel but later found the ongoing delay inexcusable when no new counsel was retained and no steps were taken after a significant period had passed (paras 22, 24). The evidence does not address the specific impact of multiple, as opposed to single, changes in counsel.

The death of a key witness has been treated as a critical factor establishing serious prejudice. In Province of New Brunswick v Clayco Construction, the court dismissed the action because the death of the defendant's "directing mind" during the period of delay was found to "likely significantly impair the ability of Clayco to defend this claim" (paras 30, 36). In general, to show serious prejudice, a party must establish that they cannot properly defend the claim due to the unavailability of witnesses, failing memory, or a similar cause (Levesque v Vitalité Health Network, para 17). The onus is on the defendant to prove prejudice, although in cases of grossly inordinate delay, prejudice may be inferred (Province of New Brunswick v Clayco Construction, para 24). However, some courts are hesitant to presume prejudice, especially based solely on the frailty of human memory (Sirois v. Boudreau, paras 8-9; Levesque v Vitalité Health Network, para 22). The nature of the claim is also relevant; if a case is based largely on documentary evidence, prejudice from delay is considered less significant (Bridgewater Bank v. Pietersma, para 13).

To oppose a motion for dismissal, the evidence suggests that parties should provide explanations for the delay through affidavit evidence. Courts have criticized the absence of affidavits to justify delays (Bridgewater Bank v. Pietersma, para 11; Sirois v. Boudreau, para 7).

Regarding the vacating of a lis pendens, referred to in the documents as a Certificate of Pending Litigation (CPL), the mechanism is a motion to the court under Rule 42.04 (MacPhee v. Macphee Estate, para 33). The legal test to vacate a CPL is very high. The court will not vacate a CPL unless it is clear that the plaintiff, even if successful in the action, cannot obtain an interest in the land in question (MacPhee v. Macphee Estate, paras 34-35). The party moving to vacate the CPL must prove that "under no possible circumstances can the facts set out in the pleadings give any right in respect of the land in question" (MacPhee v. Macphee Estate, para 35). In one case, a CPL was maintained because the plaintiffs were seeking specific performance to purchase the property, and the court could not conclude that they would fail to obtain an interest in the land if they won the case (Michaud v. Saucier, paras 46-47).

The evidence does not show a CPL being vacated solely due to litigation delay while the underlying action remained active, though delay was raised as an argument in one instance (MacPhee v. Macphee Estate, para 30). The focus of the courts has been on the nature of the claim itself. However, since a CPL is tied to a proceeding where an interest in land is questioned, it follows that if the underlying action is dismissed for delay, this constitutes a final determination of the matter, which would remove the basis for the CPL (Michaud v. Saucier, para 47). The provided evidence is insufficient to detail the specific procedural interaction between a pending motion to dismiss and a motion to vacate a CPL, but a successful dismissal motion would almost certainly lead to the CPL's removal.

query_text: What are the legal standards and factors courts consider when evaluating a motion for involuntary dismissal due to lack of diligent prosecution, particularly in cases involving attorney turnover, unforeseen delays such as public health emergencies, or the death of a material witness?
answer:
Based on the provided evidence, when a defendant moves to have an action dismissed for delay, courts in New Brunswick apply a three-part test. The defendant moving for dismissal must establish that: 1) there has been an inordinate delay; 2) the inordinate delay is inexcusable; and 3) the defendant is likely to be seriously prejudiced by the delay (Province of New Brunswick v Clayco Construction (2001) Ltd., et al,2022 NBQB 66; Francis v LeBlanc, Roy, Daigle, Desrosiers and Economical, 2025 NBKB 202). Dismissal is considered a "draconian" remedy to be exercised with caution and only in the clearest of cases (Régie régionale de la santé 6, Dr. Blanchard and Dr. Bélisle v. Robichaud,2009 NBCA 51).

Regarding the specific factors in your query:

Death of a Material Witness: The evidence shows that the death of a key witness is a significant factor in establishing serious prejudice. In Province of New Brunswick v Clayco, the court dismissed an action after a nine-year delay, during which the defendant company's key witness—described as its "directing mind" and "hands-on supervisor"—passed away. The court found that this death would "significantly impair the ability of Clayco to defend this claim" and that the prejudice was directly attributable to the delay. The argument that other witnesses or documents could substitute for the deceased's testimony was rejected (Province of New Brunswick v Clayco Construction (2001) Ltd., et al,2022 NBQB 66). This is distinct from general arguments about the frailty of human memory, which courts have found insufficient on their own to establish prejudice (Sirois v. Boudreau, 1986 CARSWELLNB 355; Levesque v Vitalité Health Network, 2019 NBQB 200).

Attorney Turnover: The evidence indicates that while attorney turnover can be a reason for delay, it does not automatically render the delay excusable. The plaintiff is ultimately considered responsible for moving the litigation forward (Francis v LeBlanc, Roy, Daigle, Desrosiers and Economical, 2025 NBKB 202). In one case, a plaintiff became self-represented after her lawyer was removed; her subsequent failure to retain new counsel or take any steps to advance the case for over a year contributed to the court finding the delay inexcusable and dismissing the action (Francis v LeBlanc, Roy, Daigle, Desrosiers and Economical, 2025 NBKB 202). In another instance, delays caused by a plaintiff's multiple changes in solicitors were also deemed inexcusable (Sirois v. Boudreau, 1986 CARSWELLNB 355). However, one court expressed concern that a plaintiff may not have been aware of procedural delays caused by their counsel, which factored into the decision not to dismiss the case (Levesque v Vitalité Health Network, 2019 NBQB 200).

Unforeseen Delays such as Public Health Emergencies: The provided evidence does not contain a case where a court evaluated a motion for involuntary dismissal for delay based primarily on an unforeseen public health emergency. This is an important detail not covered by the evidence. However, related cases offer some insight. In a civil matter concerning an extension of time for service, the court in Bridgewater Bank v. Pietersma (2021 NBQB 180) accepted that the COVID-19 pandemic created "understandable complications" and was an "exigent circumstance" that justified granting the extension, despite significant concerns about the delay. In the different context of criminal law and the constitutional right to a speedy trial, delays due to the pandemic have been recognized as "discrete exceptional circumstances" (S.J.L. v. R., 2024 NBCA 76). However, in that context, the Crown (the prosecuting party) was still required to show that it took reasonable steps to mitigate the delay. A failure to provide evidence of any mitigation efforts resulted in the court refusing to subtract the delay, leading to a stay of the charges (His Majesty the King v. Darrin Albert Donovan, 2025 NBKB 90). The insufficiency of the evidence on this point is important; while the evidence suggests a public health emergency would likely be considered a valid excuse for some period of delay, it is not clear whether a plaintiff would still need to demonstrate efforts to mitigate that delay or advance the case once it became possible to do so.

query_text: What are the general legal principles or standards that judges use to decide if a lawsuit has taken too long and should be dismissed? What kinds of reasons for delay do courts typically consider valid or excusable?
answer:
Based on the provided evidence, when judges decide if a lawsuit should be dismissed for taking too long, they apply different standards depending on whether the case is civil or criminal.

In civil cases, courts in New Brunswick have consistently applied a three-part test. To have an action dismissed for delay, a party must establish that (1) there has been an inordinate delay, (2) the delay is inexcusable, and (3) the defendant is likely to be seriously prejudiced by the delay (Francis v LeBlanc, Roy, Daigle, Desrosiers and Economical; Province of New Brunswick v Clayco Construction (2001) Ltd., et al). This is a discretionary remedy that courts use with caution, describing it as a "draconian" measure to be used only in the clearest of cases, particularly if a limitation period has expired (Régie régionale de la santé 6, Dr. Blanchard and Dr. Bélisle v. Robichaud; Province of New Brunswick v Clayco Construction (2001) Ltd., et al).

The most important factors in this analysis appear to be the reasons for the delay and the existence of prejudice.

Regarding prejudice, the moving party typically has the onus to demonstrate that they will be unable to properly defend the claim due to the delay (Province of New Brunswick v Clayco Construction (2001) Ltd., et al). Serious prejudice has been found where a key witness died during the period of delay, significantly impairing the party's ability to defend the claim (Province of New Brunswick v Clayco Construction (2001) Ltd., et al). Similarly, prejudice was found likely in a complex motor vehicle accident case with 16 potential witnesses, where memories could fail and evidence could be lost over time (Francis v LeBlanc, Roy, Daigle, Desrosiers and Economical). However, some courts have stated that prejudice cannot be established by relying solely on the general frailty of human memory (Levesque v Vitalité Health Network (Restigouche Health Authority-RSS5); Sirois v. Boudreau). The nature of the lawsuit is also a key consideration; in a case based entirely on documentary evidence, the court found the passage of time had less significance and did not prejudice the defendant's ability to mount a defense (Bridgewater Bank v. Pietersma). In cases of "grossly inordinate delay," such as a nine-year period of inaction, some courts have inferred that serious prejudice has occurred, shifting the burden to the plaintiff to prove otherwise (Province of New Brunswick v Clayco Construction (2001) Ltd., et al; Francis v LeBlanc, Roy, Daigle, Desrosiers and Economical).

In assessing whether a delay is excusable, courts have considered a range of reasons. The COVID-19 pandemic was accepted as a valid reason for delay in both civil and criminal matters, although its persuasiveness in civil cases was seen to diminish over time as court operations returned to normal (Bridgewater Bank v. Pietersma; S.J.L. v. R.). Courts have also treated significant personal challenges as a reasonable excuse, such as a plaintiff's severe health problems, cognitive difficulties, family deaths, and grief (Francis v LeBlanc, Roy, Daigle, Desrosiers and Economical; McNichol v. Co-operators General Insurance Co.). However, even compelling personal reasons may not excuse a delay indefinitely, especially if the party takes no steps to advance their case over a long period (Francis v LeBlanc, Roy, Daigle, Desrosiers and Economical). On the other hand, courts have found delays to be inexcusable when a party with significant resources claimed its legal department was too busy, or when a plaintiff simply failed to take any action to move their case forward (Province of New Brunswick v Clayco Construction (2001) Ltd., et al; Francis v LeBlanc, Roy, Daigle, Desrosiers and Economical).

In the criminal law context, a different standard known as the Jordan framework is used. This framework sets a presumptive time limit for a trial to be completed. If the delay exceeds this ceiling, it is considered presumptively unreasonable. The burden then shifts to the Crown to justify the delay by showing there were "exceptional circumstances," such as the COVID-19 pandemic, and that the Crown took all reasonable steps to mitigate the delay caused by those circumstances (His Majesty the King v. Darrin Albert Donovan; S.J.L. v. R.). A failure by the Crown to show it tried to mitigate the delay can result in the case being stayed, even if the initial cause was an exceptional event (His Majesty the King v. Darrin Albert Donovan).

The provided evidence does not contain sufficient information to determine if these exact principles apply uniformly across all Canadian provinces, as procedural rules can differ by jurisdiction. The documents are primarily from New Brunswick courts, and this jurisdictional context could be an important factor.

query_text: What are the legal standards courts use when deciding whether to dismiss a civil lawsuit due to long delays, including those caused by changes in lawyers, unexpected events, or unavailable witnesses? Specifically, what level of harm (prejudice) is needed to dismiss the case, and when might a court grant other remedies, such as removing a lis pendens, if the lawsuit is dismissed because of these delays?
answer:
Based on the provided evidence, when courts in New Brunswick consider dismissing a civil lawsuit for delay, they consistently apply a three-part test. To have an action dismissed, the moving party (usually the defendant) must establish that there has been (1) an inordinate delay, (2) the delay is inexcusable, and (3) the defendant is likely to be seriously prejudiced by the delay (Francis v LeBlanc, Roy, Daigle, Desrosiers and Economical; Province of New Brunswick v Clayco Construction (2001) Ltd., et al). Dismissal is considered a "Draconian" remedy that is used with caution and only in the clearest of cases (Régie régionale de la santé 6, Dr. Blanchard and Dr. Bélisle v. Robichaud).

The courts have examined various excuses for delay. Significant personal hardships, including serious health problems, diminished cognitive abilities, and family crises, have been found to be an acceptable explanation for a delay (McNichol v. Co-operators General Insurance Co.). The COVID-19 pandemic was also treated as an "exigent circumstance" justifying some, but not indefinite, delay (Bridgewater Bank v. Pietersma). In contrast, excuses such as a legal department being busy with other files or having a change in solicitors have been rejected (Province of New Brunswick v Clayco Construction (2001) Ltd., et al; Sirois v. Boudreau). Similarly, while a plaintiff's personal struggles like grief were viewed with empathy, they did not fully excuse a continued multi-year delay after the court had already granted an adjournment to help them get back on track (Francis v LeBlanc, Roy, Daigle, Desrosiers and Economical).

Regarding the level of harm, the moving party has the onus to demonstrate "serious prejudice," meaning their ability to make a full defense has been significantly impaired (Régie régionale de la santé 6, Dr. Blanchard and Dr. Bélisle v. Robichaud). This standard was met where a key witness for the defense died during an inexcusable nine-year delay (Province of New Brunswick v Clayco Construction (2001) Ltd., et al) and where a six-year delay in a multi-vehicle accident case created a risk of witnesses becoming unavailable or their memories fading (Francis v LeBlanc, Roy, Daigle, Desrosiers and Economical). However, courts have stated that prejudice cannot be established by relying solely on the general frailty of human memory, and there must be some evidence that witnesses are actually unavailable or their attendance is difficult to obtain (Sirois v. Boudreau; Levesque v Vitalité Health Network). In cases of "grossly inordinate" delay, some courts have found that prejudice can be inferred, shifting the burden to the plaintiff to prove otherwise, though at least one judge has expressed skepticism about this approach (Francis v LeBlanc, Roy, Daigle, Desrosiers and Economical; Levesque v Vitalité Health Network).

If a motion to dismiss is denied, a court may grant an alternative remedy, such as ordering the plaintiff to complete certain steps by a strict deadline, failing which the case will be dismissed without a further hearing (Sirois v. Boudreau; Levesque v Vitalité Health Network).

The provided evidence also addresses the standard for removing a Certificate of Pending Litigation (also known as a lis pendens). A certificate may be issued in any proceeding where a title to or interest in land is brought into question (Michaud v. Saucier; MacPhee v. Macphee Estate). The courts apply a very stringent test for removing a certificate. The moving party must prove that under no possible circumstances can the plaintiff, if successful in their lawsuit, obtain an interest in the land (MacPhee v. Macphee Estate). It is not enough to show that the plaintiff might fail in their claim; there must be a certainty that even if they win, they cannot get an interest in the land. For example, in Michaud v. Saucier, the court refused to remove a certificate where the plaintiffs sought specific performance of a purchase agreement, which could result in them obtaining an interest in the land. Similarly, in MacPhee v. Macphee Estate, a certificate was maintained even where the plaintiff’s claim to the land was indirect (as a shareholder of the company that owned the land), because it was still possible that a court order could result in her obtaining an interest in the property. The provided evidence does not contain a case where a Certificate of Pending Litigation was removed as a direct result of a lawsuit being dismissed for delay. However, the cases show that the certificate's purpose is to give notice of pending litigation that could affect title to land. If the underlying lawsuit is dismissed, the litigation is no longer pending, and the basis for the certificate would cease to exist.

query_text: My request to involve additional people in my case and get certain documents was rejected because it would cause a trial delay. The trial date then got postponed for reasons completely out of my control. Can the court still use that original rejection to stop me from making the same request now, even though the delay issue is no longer relevant?
answer:
Based on the provided evidence, courts have the jurisdiction to reconsider prior pre-trial (interlocutory) decisions, and the legal principle of res judicata (that a matter has already been judged) generally does not prevent a party from making a second procedural request. The most important factor in a court's decision to reconsider a prior ruling is whether there has been a "material change in circumstances" since the original decision was made.

A material change is one that relates to the specific reason the original order was made in the first place. The party asking for the reconsideration must show that this change has occurred and that, if it had been known at the time, the original decision would likely have been different (Canadian Broadcasting Corporation v. Canada (Border Services Agency)). In your situation, the fact that the trial date was postponed for unrelated reasons appears to be a direct change to the factual foundation of the original rejection, which was based on avoiding trial delay. Previous cases show that when a judge denies a request "at this stage of the proceeding," it may be interpreted as a dismissal without prejudice, leaving the door open for a later application if circumstances change (Global Petroleum Corp. v. Point Tupper Terminals Co.).

When the specific request involves adding new parties to a case, the court operates under a general presumption that all interested persons should be included in one hearing to avoid multiple lawsuits and save costs (Buteau v. Maritime Permanent Roofing Ltd). To block the addition of a new party, the opposing side must prove that doing so would cause them "serious, non-compensable prejudice." The evidence indicates that prejudice caused by increasing the length or complexity of a trial is generally not considered serious or non-compensable. Instead, this type of prejudice is typically evidentiary in nature, such as the loss of documents or witnesses due to the passage of time (Buteau v. Maritime Permanent Roofing Ltd). Modern Paving Ltd.; Hynes v. Professional Diving Contractors Limited). Professional Diving Contractors Limited).

The principle of proportionality is a key factor courts have used to limit discovery. Dwyer, as cited in Donovan Homes Ltd. v. Modern Paving Ltd. and Hynes v. Professional Diving Contractors Limited). Oceaneering International Inc.). Generally, the legal remedy for such a breach is a damages award that puts the claimant in the position they would have been in had the contract been properly performed (2019 BCSC 1573). Regarding the failure to provide important facts, the remedy of rescission is available for a contract induced by a false or misleading representation (2020 ONCA 304). In one case, a settlement was rescinded because certain key information provided to one party by the other was found to be false (2020 ONCA 304). query_text: Say someone gets charged with a bunch of stuff like armed robbery and driving really bad and hurting someone, plus they keep breaking court orders and probation. What kind of jail time could they be looking at for all those problems combined?

2. Supporting Arguments
Courts determine a fit sentence for each specific offence before considering the combined total. For armed robbery, a serious violent offence, the Criminal Code provides for a maximum punishment of life imprisonment (Criminal Code, RSC 1985, c C-46). If a restricted or prohibited firearm is used, a first offence carries a mandatory minimum sentence of five years (Criminal Code, RSC 1985, c C-46; 2023 SCC 3). In cases of unsophisticated robberies of commercial businesses, courts in Alberta have used three years' imprisonment as a starting point (2019 ABPC 206; 2023 SCC 3). One offender with two prior robbery convictions received a three-year sentence for his third robbery offence (2019 ABCA 496).

For dangerous driving causing bodily harm, the maximum penalty is 14 years' imprisonment (Criminal Code, RSC 1985, c C-46). A review of past cases suggests a sentencing range of 12 to 24 months is often applied, although this can vary based on the circumstances (2019 ABPC 206). In a case involving a number of offences, an offender received a 15-month sentence for dangerous driving causing bodily harm, which was ordered to be served consecutively to his sentence for robbery (2019 ABPC 206).

Failing to comply with a probation order is an offence punishable by up to four years in prison (Criminal Code, RSC 1985, c C-46). Courts have treated a history of breaches as an aggravating factor demonstrating a disregard for the justice system, often imposing consecutive sentences for these offences (2019 ABCA 496). For example, one offender with a history of 11 prior breaches received consecutive one-month sentences for new breach charges (2019 ABCA 496). Committing offences while on probation is also an aggravating factor that can increase the sentence for the primary crimes (2023 SCC 3; 2019 ABPC 206).

When an offender is sentenced for multiple crimes, the court must apply the "totality principle." This requires the judge to review the cumulative sentence to ensure it is not excessive and is proportional to the offender's overall culpability (1996 CANLII 230 SCC). If the total sentence is deemed a "crushing sentence," the court will adjust the individual sentences downward to arrive at a "just and appropriate" global sentence (1996 CANLII 230 SCC). For example, in a case involving robbery, dangerous driving, and multiple breaches, the judge first calculated sentences for each offence that added up to 6.5 years, but then reduced the final global sentence to 5.5 years based on the totality principle (2019 ABPC 206). In another matter, an offender's sentence for robbery, firearm offences, and multiple court order breaches was reduced from over five years to a total of four years, in part because of his youth (2019 ABCA 496).

These mitigating and aggravating factors significantly influence the final sentence, as they speak to the offender's degree of responsibility (2019 ABPC 206; 2016 ABPC 113).

3. Final Conclusion
In cases involving convictions for multiple serious offences such as armed robbery, dangerous driving causing bodily harm, and numerous breaches of court orders, courts establish a fit sentence for each crime individually. Previous decisions have resulted in total sentences in the range of four to six years for similar combinations of offences. Debono, 2019 ONCJ 298; 2020 ONCA 609). Jordan, 2016 SCC 27; R. v. Debono, 2019 ONCJ 298).

The framework establishes two distinct scenarios with different burdens of proof.

If the net delay exceeds the 18-month ceiling, the delay is presumed to be unreasonable. Jordan, 2016 SCC 27; R. v. Debono, 2019 ONCJ 298). A stay of proceedings for a delay below the ceiling is intended to be a rare remedy, granted only in clear cases (R. v. Jordan, 2016 SCC 27).

This involves balancing the detainee's reduced privacy interest against legitimate state objectives for the surveillance, such as detainee and officer safety, the preservation of evidence, and institutional accountability (2020 ABPC 32). This balancing has led to different results in factually similar cases.

In R v Alfreds, a court found no Charter breach when a female detainee was recorded using a cell toilet while supervised by a female officer. The court noted that the recording was not unduly intrusive as no private parts were visible and access to the video was restricted, though it did find that notice of the surveillance was deficient (2020 ABPC 32). Conversely, in R v Marty, the court upheld a finding of a Charter breach where a female detainee's bare thighs and buttocks were briefly visible on a video that was monitored by a male employee. This was found to be an objectively unreasonable intrusion (2021 ABQB 279). Similarly, a breach was found in R v Cassidy where a female detainee, who presented no specific safety risk, was monitored using the toilet (2021 ABPC 222).

When a court finds a Charter breach has occurred, it must then consider the appropriate remedy. The outcomes of this analysis have also varied drastically (2020 ABPC 32). A court may decide that no remedy is required, order the exclusion of evidence obtained following the breach, or, in the "clearest of cases," order a stay of proceedings (2021 ABQB 279). In R v Marty, the trial judge excluded the certificate of analysis, which was fatal to the Crown’s case (2021 ABQB 279). In contrast, the judges in R v Alfreds and R v Cassidy both indicated that even if a breach had occurred or was found, the exclusion of evidence would be inappropriate after balancing factors such as the seriousness of the police conduct against society's interest in having the case decided on its merits (2020 ABPC 32; 2021 ABPC 222).

The evidence provided does not outline a definitive set of rules or national standards that police must follow regarding cameras in bathrooms. Factors such as providing verbal notice of surveillance, ensuring supervision by an officer of the same gender, the actual intrusiveness of the video, and whether the detainee poses a safety risk have been identified by courts as important considerations, but their weight varies from case to case.

The case law establishes that while detainees have a diminished expectation of privacy, they retain a constitutionally protected interest in privacy during toileting activities. query_text: What are the general rules about police officers using body cameras to record strip searches during an arrest or detention? When is it considered legal or illegal for them to do that? The legal issue concerns whether video recording a strip search constitutes an unreasonable search contrary to section 8 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, and what remedy is appropriate if a court finds that a Charter right has been breached. Supporting Arguments
A strip search is considered an inherently humiliating and degrading experience that represents a significant invasion of privacy (2001 SCC 83; 2012 ABQB 656). For a strip search to be lawful, it must be authorized by law, the law itself must be reasonable, and the search must be conducted in a reasonable manner (2001 SCC 83). Police cannot conduct strip searches as a matter of routine policy; they must have reasonable and probable grounds to believe the search is necessary to find weapons or evidence related to the reason for the arrest (2001 SCC 83; 2017 ABQB 191). Because they are so intrusive, strip searches are considered prima facie unreasonable, and the Crown bears the burden of proving their legality (2003 ABPC 211).

Surreptitious video surveillance by the state constitutes a "search" within the meaning of section 8 of the Charter (1990 CANLII 56 SCC). While individuals in police custody have a diminished expectation of privacy, that expectation is not eliminated entirely (2021 ABQB 279). The manner in which a strip search is conducted is critical to its reasonableness, and the use of video recording is a key factor in this assessment. Courts have found that recording a strip search can render it unreasonable. For example, a search was found to be unreasonable where a live camera in the search room projected images to a communal police report room, with no effort made to provide privacy for the accused (2003 ABPC 211). In another case, the fact that a strip search was videotaped was a factor that contributed to the court's finding that the search was conducted unreasonably (2017 ABQB 191). The provided evidence discusses the use of fixed cameras in police stations, but it is insufficient to determine the specific rules regarding the use of body cameras worn by officers during a strip search. This distinction could be important, as the location and control of the recording device may affect the privacy analysis.

If a court concludes that a strip search was unreasonable and breached an individual's section 8 Charter rights, the evidence obtained will not automatically be excluded from trial (2017 ABQB 405). The court must conduct an analysis under section 24(2) of the Charter to determine if admitting the evidence would bring the administration of justice into disrepute. This involves balancing three factors: the seriousness of the Charter-infringing state conduct, the impact of the breach on the accused’s Charter-protected interests, and society's interest in the adjudication of the case on its merits (2017 ABQB 405; 2012 ABQB 656).

In past cases, evidence has been excluded following an improperly recorded strip search where the evidence was "conscriptive" (meaning the accused was compelled to participate in its discovery) and would not have been found otherwise, thereby rendering the trial unfair (2003 ABPC 211). However, courts have also admitted evidence even after finding a strip search was unlawful. This has occurred where the police conduct was not seen as wilful or reckless, where the impact on the accused's privacy was mitigated by the otherwise humane manner of the search, and where the evidence was reliable and crucial to a serious charge (2022 SCC 1; 2021 ABPC 222). Evidence has also been admitted where there was no direct connection between the illegal search and the evidence the Crown sought to use (2012 ABQB 656).

Final Conclusion
In previous cases, the legality of recording a strip search has been determined by whether the recording made the search unreasonable under section 8 of the Charter. Courts have considered factors such as the heightened privacy interests of the individual being searched and the justification for the recording. The presence of a video camera, particularly if it broadcasts to non-essential personnel or is used without notice, has contributed to findings that searches were unconstitutional. When a search is found to have been conducted improperly, any evidence found is not automatically excluded. A court must balance the seriousness of the police misconduct, the impact on the individual’s rights, and the public interest in having the case decided on its merits to determine whether the evidence should be admitted.

In previous cases involving multiple offences, courts have determined sentences by applying the fundamental principle of proportionality, which is shaped by a balancing of aggravating and mitigating factors specific to the offence and the offender. Once issued, a publication ban is broad in scope, covering any information that "could identify" the protected person, and it remains in full force indefinitely, continuing even in subsequent civil proceedings (2017 ONSC 5650). 3. Final Conclusion

For other offences, including what would likely be non-sexual assault domestic violence matters, the process is discretionary and requires a judge to balance the need for confidentiality against the principle of open courts. answer:

This response addresses the law surrounding police searches of vehicles under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. The jurisprudence indicates that the lawfulness of any search is critically dependent on the lawfulness of the arrest that precedes it and the specific purpose for which the police conduct the search.

2. Supporting Arguments

The legality of a vehicle search has been consistently tied to the legality of the occupant's arrest. A search incident to arrest is invalid if the arrest itself is unlawful (2011 SCC 21). An arrest has been found to be unlawful and arbitrary if it is based on an officer's mistake of law, such as believing a legal substance was a controlled drug, even if the substance was seen in plain view (2022 SCC 12). The evidence provided is insufficient to detail the rules governing plain view observations from outside a vehicle, particularly in circumstances where an officer's initial suspicion has been dispelled. This is a potentially important detail, as continued detention or observation after reasonable suspicion has been eliminated could itself constitute a Charter breach.

For a search of a vehicle to be lawfully incidental to an arrest, it must be "truly incidental to the arrest" (1998 CANLII 838 SCC). This requires the police to have a valid purpose connected to the arrest, such as protecting the police or public, preserving evidence, or discovering evidence of the offence for which the arrest was made. Police must have a subjective reason for the search that is related to the arrest, and this reason must be objectively reasonable (1998 CANLII 838 SCC). A search conducted for a purpose unrelated to the arrest, such as a routine inventory search pursuant to a police policy, has been found to fall outside the scope of this common law power (1998 CANLII 838 SCC).

With respect to temporal and spatial limits, the courts have held that delay and distance do not automatically invalidate a search incident to arrest. A search conducted six hours after an arrest at a separate impound lot has been considered. However, a significant delay may cause a court to infer that the search was not sufficiently connected to the arrest, though this inference can be rebutted with a proper explanation (1998 CANLII 838 SCC). The provided evidence does not address the specific circumstance of keys being discovered post-arrest, but the established principles suggest any subsequent search would still need to be justified as being truly incidental to the original arrest.

Even when a search is found to be unlawful and in breach of the Charter, the evidence obtained is not automatically excluded. The evidence will be excluded only if its admission would bring the administration of justice into disrepute (2022 SCC 12). This is determined by balancing three factors: the seriousness of the Charter-infringing state conduct, the impact of the breach on the accused's Charter-protected interests, and society's interest in the adjudication of the case on its merits (2022 SCC 12). In past cases, Charter breaches have been considered less serious when they resulted from an "honest mistake" of law by an officer or were conducted in good faith, even if unlawfully (2022 SCC 12; 1998 CANLII 838 SCC). The impact on an individual's rights has been considered moderate in the context of a vehicle search due to a lesser expectation of privacy, and society's interest in an adjudication on the merits is high when the evidence is reliable and essential for prosecuting serious offences (2022 SCC 12; 1998 CANLII 838 SCC).

3. Final Conclusion

In summary, the lawfulness of a vehicle search incident to arrest is contingent upon a lawful arrest. The search must be conducted for a valid purpose connected to the reasons for the arrest, not for an unrelated administrative reason. While temporal and spatial separation between the arrest and the search are permitted, they can weaken the required connection. If a search is found to have violated an individual's Charter rights, the evidence will only be suppressed if a balancing of the seriousness of the state conduct, the impact on the individual, and society's interest in the case leads to the conclusion that admitting the evidence would bring the administration of justice into disrepute.

Guilt by association or mere passive acquiescence is not sufficient for a conviction (R v Moore). The standard of proof is different depending on the stage of the legal process. For a person to be committed to stand trial following a preliminary inquiry, the test is whether there is any evidence upon which a reasonable jury could potentially convict, meaning guilt is a reasonable inference from the evidence (R v Ormrod). For a conviction at trial, the standard is higher, requiring proof beyond a reasonable doubt that guilt is the only reasonable inference (R v Gattie & Mohammed).

In cases where no drugs were found on a person, the courts have focused on the strength of the circumstantial evidence linking the individual to the drugs found at a property. A key factor is the individual's connection to the premises. In R v Ormrod, being the leaseholder of the property was significant evidence contributing to the accused being committed for trial, as a jury could reasonably infer that the leaseholder had access to and control over the entire premises. However, at the trial stage, simply being the tenant may not be enough for a conviction if there is no specific evidence linking the accused to the drugs. In R v Gattie & Mohammed, the tenant of an apartment was acquitted because the drugs were found in a locked bedroom to which he was not demonstrably connected, and the court could not be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that he had the necessary control, despite strong suspicions.

The most important evidence in these cases has been that which specifically connects an individual to the drugs or the precise location of the drugs within a property. For instance, a conviction was secured against one accused in R v Gattie & Mohammed because bank receipts and cellphone data directly linked him to the locked bedroom where the drugs were found, establishing his occupation of that specific room and, by inference, his knowledge and control over its contents. Similarly, in R v Mohamed, an occupant was convicted where drugs were found in plain view between his legs upon arrest in a bathroom he clearly used, and other drugs were on a living room table next to his personal items like sunglasses.

Conversely, a lack of evidence demonstrating control has led to acquittals, even where knowledge was established. In R v Moore, the accused was acquitted because although the court was satisfied he knew or was willfully blind to the presence of drugs in a vehicle, there was no evidence he had any measure of control over them; he did not help hide them or direct their transport.

Observations of routine activities, such as entering and leaving a premises, are used to establish a person's connection to that location as an occupant. However, the evidence suggests these observations alone are not sufficient for a conviction. In R v Gattie & Mohammed, surveillance showed both accused coming and going from the apartment building, but this only served as a starting point. The conviction of one and acquittal of the other depended entirely on the further evidence linking them, or failing to link them, to the specific room containing the drugs. The provided evidence does not contain a case where a conviction was based solely on an individual's association with a property and observations of routine activities. The absence of further evidence directly tying an accused to the narcotics, which proves the crucial element of control, appears to be a determining factor at trial.

query_text: What are the legal rules or factors that determine if someone can be found to have 'joint possession' of drugs and an 'intention to traffic,' especially when the drugs weren't found right on them, but rather on a property they were connected to?
answer:
1. Opening Statements

This research synthesizes judicial interpretations of criminal possession, specifically concerning illegal drugs. The query asks for the legal rules and factors that courts have used to determine if an individual had 'joint possession' of drugs and an 'intention to traffic,' especially when the drugs were located on a property linked to the accused rather than on their person. Based on the provided documents, courts require the prosecution to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused had both knowledge of the drugs and a measure of control over them, and these elements are determined through a careful analysis of the totality of the evidence in each case.

2. Supporting Arguments

Under the Criminal Code, a person can be in personal, constructive, or joint possession of an item (R. v. Morelli, (2010 SCC 8)). For all forms of possession, the essential elements of knowledge and control must be proven (R. v. Morelli, (2010 SCC 8)). Joint possession is addressed in section 4(3)(b) of the Criminal Code, which deems an item to be in the possession of multiple people when one person has it with the knowledge and consent of the others (R. v. Terrence, (1983 CANLII 51 SCC)). Courts have consistently held that to establish this form of possession, the Crown must prove that each accused person had some measure of control over the item (R. v. Terrence, (1983 CANLII 51 SCC); R v Moore, (2012 NWTSC 36)). Mere presence at a location where drugs are found, or passive acquiescence to their presence, is not sufficient to establish the necessary control or consent (R. v. Terrence, (1983 CANLII 51 SCC); R v Moore, (2012 NWTSC 36)). For example, being a passenger in a vehicle containing illegal items does not, on its own, prove possession without evidence that the passenger exercised some form of control (R. v. Terrence, (1983 CANLII 51 SCC)).

When drugs are found in a residence, a court may be entitled to infer that an occupant was aware of and had control over drugs found within the premises (R v Gattie & Mohammed, (2020 NWTSC 11); R v Mohamed, (2018 NWTSC 64)). The strength of this inference depends on a range of factors, including whether the accused lived at the property, who paid the rent, the presence of their personal effects, and their frequency of attendance (R v Gattie & Mohammed, (2020 NWTSC 11); R v Mohamed, (2018 NWTSC 64)). An occupant's knowledge and control can often be inferred when drugs are left in plain view in common areas of the home, such as a living room or kitchen (R v Mohamed, (2018 NWTSC 64)). However, establishing a connection between an accused and the property is not always enough. There must be a nexus between the accused and the specific drugs seized; simply being part of a conspiracy to traffic or being associated with others who possess drugs is insufficient to prove possession (R. v. Venneri, (2012 SCC 33)). In one case, the tenant of an apartment was acquitted because the drugs were found in a locked bedroom that was primarily occupied by others, and the evidence did not prove his knowledge and control beyond a reasonable doubt (R v Gattie & Mohammed, (2020 NWTSC 11)).

An intention to traffic is often inferred from circumstantial evidence. The quantity of drugs found is a primary factor; if the amount is greater than what would be for personal use, an inference of trafficking may be drawn (R v McLean, (2014 NWTSC 9)). This inference is strengthened by the presence of other evidence associated with drug trafficking, such as large sums of cash, digital scales, packaging materials, score sheets, and weapons (R v Mohamed, (2018 NWTSC 64); R v Ormrod, (2014 NWTTC 26)). Evidence that an accused was involved in a drug trafficking operation can also support an inference that they had knowledge and control of firearms found on the property, as dealers often use weapons for protection (R v Ormrod, (2014 NWTTC 26)). The evidence provided focuses heavily on defining the elements of possession in general (knowledge and control) and applying them to residential scenarios but does not contain extensive judicial analysis distinguishing a finding of 'joint possession' from 'constructive possession' among multiple accused. This distinction could be important in determining the nature of each person's culpability in a shared space.

3. Final Conclusion

To establish joint possession of drugs found on a property, previous court decisions indicate that the Crown must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that each accused person knew the drugs were there and had some measure of control over them. A person's status as a resident or occupant can be used to infer knowledge and control, particularly over drugs found in common areas, but mere presence or association with the property is not sufficient. Intention to traffic is typically established through inferences drawn from the quantity of drugs seized and the presence of paraphernalia associated with a drug-selling operation.

query_text: How do appellate courts typically address instances where a trial judge makes an error of law regarding the substantive elements of a criminal offense, but the defense failed to preserve that error for appeal?

Jacquard, (1997 CANLII 374 SCC); R. v. McIntosh, (2024 BCCA 292)). The ultimate responsibility for ensuring the legal correctness of a trial, including the instructions to a jury, rests with the trial judge, not counsel (R. v. Jacquard, (1997 CANLII 374 SCC); R. v. Abdullahi, (2023 SCC 19)). To treat a failure to object as a waiver of appeal rights could prejudice an accused, particularly in cases where counsel is inexperienced (R. v. Jacquard, (1997 CANLII 374 SCC)).

Nevertheless, counsel's silence at trial has been deemed an important factor for an appellate court to consider as part of a functional review of the trial as a whole (R. v. Goforth, (2022 SCC 2); R. v. Abdullahi, (2023 SCC 19)). A failure to object may suggest that the alleged error was not considered serious at the time, and it can undermine a subsequent argument that the jury was confused or misled by the instruction (R. v. Jacquard, (1997 CANLII 374 SCC); R. v. Goforth, (2022 SCC 2)). The significance of the failure to object has been found to be greater when trial counsel had an opportunity to review the issue, such as in a pre-charge conference, or where counsel specifically endorsed the instruction that is later challenged on appeal (R. v. McIntosh, (2024 BCCA 292)).

Appellate courts have also considered the potential reason for counsel’s silence. Where there are indications that the failure to object was a tactical decision from which the defence may have hoped to benefit, courts have assigned it significant weight (R. v. Abdullahi, (2023 SCC 19)). Conversely, where the record indicates the silence was a clear oversight and not a tactical choice, it has been given little or no weight in the appellate analysis (R. v. Roche-Garcia, (2024 BCCA 298)). Finally, counsel’s failure to object has also been considered when determining whether to apply the curative proviso, as it may suggest that an established error of law was harmless in the circumstances (R. v. Abdullahi, (2023 SCC 19)).

The provided evidence is insufficient to fully answer all aspects of the query. The documents focus almost exclusively on errors arising in the context of a trial judge's instructions to a jury. This distinction could be important, as much of the analysis in the evidence relates to the potential for an error to mislead a lay jury, a factor not present in judge-alone trials.

3. Final Conclusion
In summary, appellate courts have consistently held that a failure by defence counsel to object to a legal error at trial does not bar an appeal on that issue. However, counsel’s silence is treated as a significant contextual factor. Its weight depends on the circumstances, including whether the silence appeared to be a tactical choice or a simple oversight, and what it implies about the seriousness of the error and its impact on the trial. The primary procedural mechanism identified in the case law to address a conviction in these circumstances is an appeal based on a miscarriage of justice under s. 686(1)(a)(iii) of the Criminal Code (R. v. Moazami, (2021 BCCA 328)). A miscarriage of justice occurs when an error deprives the accused of their right to a fair trial, and it can be established by showing the trial was unfair in fact or that the proceedings created an appearance of unfairness that would shake public confidence in the administration of justice (R. v. Moazami, (2021 BCCA 328)).

Ineffective assistance of counsel is a recognized ground that can produce a miscarriage of justice (R. v. Moazami, (2021 BCCA 328); R. v. Crawford, (2025 BCCA 17)). To succeed on this ground, an appellant must establish three things: the factual basis for the claim, that counsel's actions or omissions constituted incompetence, and that the incompetence caused a miscarriage of justice (R. v. Mehl, (2021 BCCA 264)). The performance component is assessed against a standard of reasonableness, and there is a strong presumption that counsel's conduct was competent and fell within the wide range of acceptable trial strategy (R. v. Crawford, (2025 BCCA 17)).

The prejudice component requires showing a link between counsel's incompetence and a miscarriage of justice (R. v. Mehl, (2021 BCCA 264)). This can be established in several ways, including by showing there is a reasonable probability that the outcome of the trial would have been different but for counsel's errors (R. v. Moazami, (2021 BCCA 328)). A reasonable probability is defined as one sufficient to undermine confidence in the verdict (R. v. Mehl, (2021 BCCA 264)). Alternatively, a miscarriage of justice can be established if counsel's performance rendered the trial process itself unfair, regardless of whether the verdict was reliable (R. v. Mehl, (2021 BCCA 264); R. v. Crawford, (2025 BCCA 17)). Applying the wrong liability standard, such as a strict liability standard for an offence requiring proof of mens rea, is a fundamental error of law (R. v. Mossman, (2026 BCCA 75); R. v. Abdullahi, (2023 SCC 19)). An appellate court may give little weight to the failure to object if it did not appear to be a tactical decision and offered no advantage to the defence (R. v. Roche-Garcia, (2024 BCCA 298)). In an ineffective assistance claim, counsel's failure to object is not viewed as a procedural bar, but rather as the very evidence of the allegedly incompetent performance. query_text: Okay, so I was charged for something, and the judge during my trial, like, totally messed up on the instructions he gave to the jury about what they needed to prove. He told them they just needed to believe I did the act, but then later everyone agreed he should have told them they also needed to believe I *intended* to do it. But the appeals court said it didn't matter because they thought there was still enough evidence to convict me anyway, even with the wrong instructions. How can a judge's legal mistake not make a difference? I'm worried this means I'm stuck with this conviction even though there was a real legal error. Isn't that unfair if the judge got the law wrong about my charge?
answer:
1. Opening Statements
This response addresses the legal principles surrounding appellate review of a trial judge's instructions to a jury in Canadian criminal law. The query concerns how a criminal conviction can be upheld by an appeal court even after it has been established that the trial judge made a legal error when instructing the jury on the elements of the offence. Based on the provided materials, while such an error can be grounds for ordering a new trial, a conviction may still be upheld if the appellate court determines the error did not cause a substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice.

2. Supporting Arguments
When an appellate court reviews a judge’s instructions to a jury, it does not demand perfection (R. v. McIntosh, (2024 BCCA 292)). The court applies a "functional approach," examining the instructions as a whole within the context of the entire trial to determine if the jury was properly equipped to decide the case according to the law and the evidence (R. v. Abdullahi, (2023 SCC 19); R. v. McIntosh, (2024 BCCA 292)).

The first step in an appeal from a conviction is for the appellant to demonstrate that the judge made an error of law, such as giving an inaccurate instruction (a "misdirection") or failing to give a necessary one (a "non-direction") (R. v. Abdullahi, (2023 SCC 19); R. v. Kruk, (2024 SCC 7)). A challenge to a judge's jury instructions is analyzed as a potential error of law (R. v. Abdullahi, (2023 SCC 19)).

If an error of law is found, the appeal is not automatically successful. The legal analysis then proceeds to a second, distinct stage involving what is known as the "curative proviso" (R. v. Abdullahi, (2023 SCC 19); R. v. Kruk, (2024 SCC 7)). At this stage, the burden shifts to the Crown to prove that the conviction should stand despite the error. The Crown can do this by satisfying the court that either the error was "harmless" or that the evidence against the accused was so "overwhelming" that the verdict would necessarily have been the same even if the error had not been made (R. v. Kruk, (2024 SCC 7)). This provision acknowledges the accused's right to a properly instructed jury but allows a verdict to be saved where the error did not result in a miscarriage of justice (R. v. Abdullahi, (2023 SCC 19)).

Courts also consider whether the defence lawyer objected to the instructions at trial. While the judge is ultimately responsible for the correctness of the law given to the jury, a failure to object is a relevant factor for the appeal court (R. v. Goforth, (2022 SCC 2); R. v. Abdullahi, (2023 SCC 19)). It may suggest that, at the time, the error was not considered serious or that counsel made a strategic choice not to raise it (R. v. Jacquard, (1997 CANLII 374 SCC); R. v. Abdullahi, (2023 SCC 19)). However, counsel's silence is not a determining factor and may be given little weight if it was clearly an oversight rather than a tactical decision (R. v. Goforth, (2022 SCC 2); R. v. Roche-Garcia, (2024 BCCA 298)).

The provided evidence is insufficient to analyze the specific error in your case concerning the element of intent or to evaluate the strength of the evidence against you. These details would be critical in a real case, as the nature of the error and the weight of the evidence are central to an appellate court’s decision on whether an error was harmless or the case was overwhelming.

3. Final Conclusion
In summary, the law allows a conviction to be upheld despite a legal error in the judge's jury instructions through a two-step process. First, the appellate court must be convinced that an error of law occurred. Second, if an error is established, the Crown may still persuade the court to dismiss the appeal by proving that the error was harmless or that the case against the accused was so overwhelming that the verdict would have been the same regardless of the mistake. This legal framework, known as the curative proviso, explains how a conviction may stand even when a legal error was made during the trial.

query_text: When a judge decides if a young person who committed a serious crime should be sentenced as an adult, what factors are important in determining if a youth sentence would be long enough to both hold them accountable and help them change to prevent future harm?
answer:
1. Opening Statements
The provided legal documents address the principles of sentencing under Canada's Youth Criminal Justice Act (YCJA) when a young person has committed a serious crime. The query concerns the factors a court considers when deciding if a youth sentence would be of sufficient length to hold a young person accountable and promote their rehabilitation, which is a key part of the legal test for imposing a more severe adult sentence. The evidence indicates that this determination is the second part of a two-step analysis and involves a discretionary and evaluative weighing of various factors related to the offence, the offender, and the fundamental principles of youth justice.

2. Supporting Arguments
Before a court considers the sufficiency of a youth sentence, the Crown must first satisfy the court that the presumption of the young person’s diminished moral blameworthiness has been rebutted, which involves proving beyond a reasonable doubt that the youth had the developmental age and maturity of an adult at the time of the offence (R. v. I.M., (2025 SCC 23)). Only after this first step is met does the court proceed to the second inquiry, which is whether a youth sentence would be of sufficient length to hold the young person accountable for their actions (R. v. S.B., (2025 SCC 24)).

This second inquiry is described as an evaluative and discretionary exercise, similar to the process of determining a fit sentence for an adult (R. v. I.M., (2025 SCC 23); R. v. S.B., (2025 SCC 24)). The concept of "accountability" under the YCJA is not solely about retribution; it is defined by the goal of imposing just sanctions with meaningful consequences that also promote the young person's rehabilitation and reintegration into society, thereby contributing to the long-term protection of the public (R. v. I.M., (2025 SCC 23); R. v. S.B., (2025 SCC 24)). In making this determination, courts have balanced a number of factors.

A central factor is the gravity or seriousness of the offence and the young person's degree of responsibility for it (R. v. I.M., (2025 SCC 23)). This includes the harm caused to victims and the community, the offender's specific role in the crime, and any post-offence conduct, such as attempts to hide evidence or deflect blame (R. v. M.W., (2017 ONCA 2); R. v. S.B., (2025 SCC 24)).

Courts also conduct an individualized assessment of the young offender's circumstances. This involves examining their background, character, prior criminal record, and personal situation, including family life, substance use, and any diagnosed disorders (R. v. M.W., (2017 ONCA 2)). A young person’s social context, including difficult upbringings or experiences with systemic discrimination, has been considered relevant to understanding their moral culpability (R. v. S.B., (2025 SCC 24); R. v. I.M., (2025 SCC 23)). The court also considers the young person's needs for rehabilitation and their potential for reintegration, which can be informed by their behaviour while in custody and by psychiatric or pre-sentence reports assessing their risk of reoffending and amenability to treatment (R. v. M.W., (2017 ONCA 2)). The availability and perceived effectiveness of specific youth programs, such as an Intensive Rehabilitative Custody and Supervision (IRCS) order, have also been weighed in the analysis (R. v. M.W., (2017 ONCA 2)).

The evidence does not provide an exhaustive list of all possible factors, as the inquiry is highly contextual and discretionary. However, it is clear that courts undertake a broad assessment to determine if the case is an exception to the general rule that a youth sentence is sufficient to achieve the goals of the YCJA (R. v. S.B., (2025 SCC 24)).

3. Final Conclusion
In summary, the judicial determination of whether a youth sentence is of sufficient length to hold a young person accountable is a discretionary balancing process that occurs only after the Crown has proven the youth possessed adult-like maturity. This inquiry requires the court to weigh factors related to the seriousness of the offence and the harm caused against the individual circumstances, moral culpability, and rehabilitative needs of the young offender. The ultimate decision is guided by the YCJA's principles, which define accountability as a concept that includes not only proportionate punishment but also the promotion of rehabilitation and reintegration to ensure long-term public safety.

query_text: What is the process a judge goes through to decide if a young person who committed a serious crime should be sentenced as an adult, and how do they determine if a youth sentence would be long enough to both hold them accountable and help them change to prevent future harm?
answer:
1. Opening Statements

This topic concerns the legal framework for sentencing young persons as adults under Canada's Youth Criminal Justice Act (YCJA). The query asks about the judicial process for determining whether a young person who has committed a serious crime should receive an adult sentence, and how a court assesses if a youth sentence is sufficient for accountability and rehabilitation. Based on the evidence, Canadian courts have established a distinct two-part test that the Crown must satisfy before a judge can impose an adult sentence on a young person.

2. Supporting Arguments

When the Crown applies to have a young person sentenced as an adult, the court engages in a two-pronged analysis set out in section 72 of the YCJA (R. v. I.M., (2025 SCC 23); R. v. M.W., (2017 ONCA 2)). These two parts are considered separate and sequential inquiries (R. v. S.B., (2025 SCC 24)).

The first prong requires the Crown to rebut the constitutionally protected presumption of a young person’s diminished moral blameworthiness or culpability (R. v. I.M., (2025 SCC 23); R. v. M.W., (2017 ONCA 2)). The onus is on the Crown to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the presumption does not apply (R. v. S.B., (2025 SCC 24); R. v. I.M., (2025 SCC 23)). This stage is a factual inquiry focused on the young person’s “developmental age” at the time of the offence. The Crown must show that the young person possessed the maturity, moral sophistication, and capacity for independent judgment of an adult (R. v. S.B., (2025 SCC 24); R. v. I.M., (2025 SCC 23)). Factors considered include the youth's personal circumstances, background, mental health, and sophistication (R. v. I.M., (2025 SCC 23)). Social context evidence, such as experiences with systemic discrimination, may also provide insight into a youth's development and moral culpability (R. v. S.B., (2025 SCC 24); R. v. I.M., (2025 SCC 23)). The objective seriousness or gravity of the crime itself is not a relevant factor in this first inquiry (R. v. S.B., (2025 SCC 24); R. v. I.M., (2025 SCC 23)).

If, and only if, the Crown has rebutted the presumption, the court proceeds to the second prong of the test. Here, the court must be satisfied that a youth sentence would not be of sufficient length to hold the young person accountable for their offending behaviour (R. v. S.B., (2025 SCC 24); R. v. I.M., (2025 SCC 23)). This part of the analysis is an evaluative and discretionary exercise, akin to determining a fit sentence, and does not require proof beyond a reasonable doubt (R. v. S.B., (2025 SCC 24); R. v. I.M., (2025 SCC 23)). At this stage, the court weighs a broader range of factors, including the seriousness of the offence, proportionality, the degree of responsibility of the offender, the harm caused to victims, and societal values (R. v. S.B., (2025 SCC 24); R. v. M.W., (2017 ONCA 2)). Accountability under the YCJA is defined as holding a young person responsible through just sanctions that have meaningful consequences and promote their rehabilitation and reintegration, thereby contributing to the long-term protection of the public (R. v. I.M., (2025 SCC 23); R. v. M.W., (2017 ONCA 2)). The court assesses whether the maximum available youth sentence, such as a ten-year sentence for first degree murder, is sufficient to meet these objectives (R. v. I.M., (2025 SCC 23)).

3. Final Conclusion

In summary, the judicial process for sentencing a young person as an adult is a structured, two-step analysis. First, a court must conduct a factual inquiry to determine if the Crown has proven beyond a reasonable doubt that the young person had the developmental maturity of an adult at the time of the offence, an analysis that must not consider the objective gravity of the crime. If this high threshold is met, the court then undertakes a discretionary assessment, weighing a variety of factors including the offence's seriousness, to decide if the legislated youth sentences are sufficiently long to achieve the YCJA's goals of accountability, rehabilitation, and long-term public protection.

query_text: What is the evidentiary standard required for the Crown to demonstrate that a youth sentence would be insufficient to achieve accountability and rehabilitation, thereby warranting an adult sentence for a young person who has committed a serious crime?
answer:
1. Opening Statements

This analysis concerns the legal framework for sentencing a young person as an adult under Canada's Youth Criminal Justice Act (YCJA). Based on the jurisprudence, the process involves a two-part test with distinct evidentiary standards for each part, with the onus of proof resting entirely on the Crown.

2. Supporting Arguments

To impose an adult sentence, the Crown must satisfy a two-pronged test set out in section 72(1) of the YCJA (R. v. I.M., (2025 SCC 23); R. v. M.W., (2017 ONCA 2)). These two prongs are distinct inquiries and must be analyzed separately (R. v. I.M., (2025 SCC 23); R. v. M.W., (2017 ONCA 2)).

The first prong, under s. 72(1)(a), requires the Crown to rebut the constitutionally protected presumption of a young person's diminished moral blameworthiness or culpability (R. v. S.B., (2025 SCC 24); R. v. M.W., (2017 ONCA 2)). This is a factual inquiry into whether the young person, at the time of the offence, had the developmental age, maturity, and capacity for moral judgment of an adult (R. v. I.M., (2025 SCC 23)). Because rebutting this presumption is akin to proving an aggravating factor that exposes the youth to a significantly more severe sentence, the Crown must prove this fact beyond a reasonable doubt (R. v. S.B., (2025 SCC 24); R. v. I.M., (2025 SCC 23)). The inquiry is offender-centric, and factors like the objective seriousness of the offence are not relevant to this determination (R. v. I.M., (2025 SCC 23)). Instead, courts consider personal circumstances such as the youth’s background, mental health, cognitive abilities, and social context (R. v. I.M., (2025 SCC 23)).

If the Crown succeeds in rebutting the presumption beyond a reasonable doubt, it must then satisfy the second prong under s. 72(1)(b): that a youth sentence would not be of sufficient length to hold the young person accountable (R. v. S.B., (2025 SCC 24)). This inquiry does not require proof beyond a reasonable doubt. Instead, it is an evaluative and discretionary task for the sentencing judge, similar to determining a fit sentence (R. v. I.M., (2025 SCC 23); R. v. S.B., (2025 SCC 24)). At this stage, the court engages in a weighing and balancing of relevant factors, including the gravity of the offence, the harm caused, societal values, and the offender's personal circumstances and rehabilitative needs (R. v. S.B., (2025 SCC 24)). The concept of accountability in the YCJA is broad, incorporating not just retribution but also the promotion of the youth's rehabilitation and reintegration into society (R. v. I.M., (2025 SCC 23); R. v. M.W., (2017 ONCA 2)).

3. Final Conclusion

In summary, the jurisprudence establishes a clear two-stage analysis for applications to sentence a young person as an adult. The Crown bears the onus of proof for both stages. First, the Crown must prove beyond a reasonable doubt the factual matter that the young person possessed the developmental maturity of an adult at the time of the offence, thereby rebutting the presumption of diminished moral blameworthiness. Second, if that high standard is met, the Crown must then satisfy the court, through an evaluative and discretionary weighing of factors, that a youth sentence would be of insufficient length to achieve the YCJA's goals of accountability, which include rehabilitation and reintegration.

The amendments in that case were found to have raised "nothing new of any substance" (2018 ONSC 1096).

However, the situation may be different if the new charges are not the same as, or included in, the original offences. A person in custody can seek a review of their detention order if there has been a "material and relevant change in the circumstances of the case" (2015 SCC 27; 2022 ONSC 6373). The addition of new charges has been explicitly recognized as such a material change. For example, when the Crown added a significant number of new charges against an accused who was already detained, the court treated it as a material change of circumstances that warranted a bail review (R v McLeod, 2016 ONSC 3793). Similarly, the withdrawal of charges that had led to an accused's bail being cancelled was also found to be a material change sufficient to trigger a review hearing (2022 ONSC 6373).

It is crucial to note that establishing a material change in circumstances does not guarantee release. The new charges may weaken the accused's position. In one instance, the addition of new charges, while qualifying as a material change, was found to increase the concerns for public safety and thereby strengthen the case for continued detention on the secondary and tertiary grounds (R v McLeod, 2016 ONSC 3793). The reviewing court will undertake a fresh assessment based on the totality of the new circumstances, including the gravity of the new alleged offences (R v McLeod, 2016 ONSC 3793).

The provided evidence is insufficient to answer what happens when a prosecutor re-lays a charge that had previously been withdrawn. This could be an important detail, as the circumstances of the withdrawal and re-laying of the charge could influence a court's decision, but based on the principles discussed, it would likely be analyzed as a material change in circumstances.

3. Final Conclusion

In summary, an accused person detained in custody is not automatically entitled to a new bail hearing if the Crown simply replaces the charging document with one charging the same or an included offence. However, the addition of completely new and different charges has been held to be a material and relevant change in circumstances. This change can provide a basis to seek a bail review hearing where a judge will reassess the need for detention, but this reassessment does not guarantee release and may, depending on the new allegations, reinforce the decision to keep the accused in custody.

It is important to note that under the Criminal Code, if a new information or indictment is laid that charges the "same offence or an included offence" as the original charges, the existing detention order automatically continues to apply (Criminal Code, RSC 1985, c C-46). If a court finds there has been a material change, it is authorized to conduct a new hearing and a fresh analysis of whether detention is still justified (R. v. J.A., 2020 ONCA 660). At the new hearing, the accused bears the onus to show on a balance of probabilities that their detention is no longer necessary (R. v. J.A., 2020 ONCA 660).
